newsitem.title: ABU DHABI: Saudi mulls opening bourse more to investors.
newsitem.headline: Saudi mulls opening bourse more to investors.

text.p: Saudi Arabia is actively reviewing its bourse, including possible measures to further open its doors to foreign and Gulf Arab investors, the kingdom's finance minister said on Saturday.

"It's clear that we are gradually calculating the moves to open up the market. We want to get the advantages of opening up the market without the disadvantages, the volatility," Ibrahim Abdel Aziz al-Asaf told Reuters.
"We are moving in the direction of openness, but at the same time we want to make sure we will do it the right way".
Asaf said the kingdom was considering gradually opening up its bourse, the biggest in the oil-rich Gulf, to internationl investors by approving further equity funds in which foreigners can own units.

Saudi American Bank (SAMBA), 30 percent owned by Citibank in March received Central Bank approval to set up the Saudi Arabian Investment Fund Ltd -- the first fund to allow foreign participation in the bourse. The market is so far restricted to Saudis and other Gulf Arabs.
"This is obviously the first closed-ended fund and we might have more of these...," Asaf said on the sidelines of an annual meeting of Arab finance ministers and central bank governors.
The closed-end fund, the size of which has yet to be announced, will be listed on the London Stock Exchange.
Analysts have predicted the SAMBA fund would usher in similar funds, for which some banks are awaiting central bank approval.
They said that foreign participation in the Saudi bourse could stem the flow of billions of dollars remitted every year by the six million expatriates in the kingdom and improve liquidity.
Only Saudi nationals can hold shares in all of the over 70 listed local firms, capitalised at some $45 billion.

Nationals of Saudi Arabia's five other partners in the Gulf Cooperation Council, an political and economic alliance grouping Bahrain, Qatar, Oman, the United Arab Emirates and Kuwait, can own Saudi equities excluding banks -- which account for about a third of market capitalisation.
Asaf said the kingdom was also considering ways of easing restrictions on Gulf Arab investors.

"We are also looking into facilitating the (wider) trading of the GCC citizens in our stock market," he said. "The GCC citizens are allowed to trade in the market but now we want to make it easier for them to do that," he added.
"These are all concrete steps in addition to the review of the whole capital market of Saudi Arabia," he added.
